title: Who Can Bring Me Down?
subtitle: Obadiah 1
description: God summons the nations against proud Edom, nested in the cliffs and certain no one can bring it down.
paragraphs: The shortest book in the Bible is a single vision against a single nation. “This is the vision of Obadiah”, it begins, and it names no king and no year for itself; the day it describes is Jerusalem's disaster, when strangers entered the city's gate, and it is told here in that company. Its subject is Edom, the nation descended from Esau, which makes everything in it a family matter: Edom is Jacob's brother grown into a country, settled in the mountain country south of Judah, in cliffs and heights that had never been taken. The vision is not long. It does not need to be. It is an announcement that the untakeable place is about to be taken apart.

The announcement opens in the council of nations. “We have heard a message from the LORD”, the vision says, and an envoy has already been sent among the nations carrying one sentence: “Rise up, and let us go to battle against her!” Before Edom hears a word of its own judgment, the armies are being summoned to deliver it. God's verdict on the mountain nation is stated first and plainly: “Behold, I will make you small among the nations; you will be deeply despised.” Small and despised, for a people whose whole security was being neither.

The charge underneath the verdict is pride, and it is described as self-deception. “The pride of your heart has deceived you, O dwellers in the clefts of the rocks whose habitation is the heights.” The cliffs were real, and the safety they gave was real, and the conclusion Edom drew from them was the lie: “Who can bring me down to the ground?” God answers the question in the form it was asked. “Though you soar like the eagle and make your nest among the stars, even from there I will bring you down.” Height is no argument. The eagle's altitude and the star's distance are named only to be crossed.

What is coming will not be an ordinary plundering, and the vision measures it by what ordinary plunderers leave behind. “If thieves came to you”, God says, “would they not steal only what they wanted?” Robbers take enough and go. Grape gatherers in a vineyard leave gleanings on the vine for the poor. Edom's ruin gets the cry, “oh, how you will be ruined”, because its plunderers will observe neither limit: “But how Esau will be pillaged, his hidden treasures sought out!” Nothing reserved, nothing overlooked, the strongboxes found and emptied. The nation that lived by being unreachable will be searched like a house whose every hiding place is known.

And the hands that help do it will be familiar ones. “All the men allied with you will drive you to the border”, God says; the partners will expel him, and the men at peace with him will deceive and overpower him. “Those who eat your bread will set a trap for you without your awareness of it.” Table companions become the trap. The wisdom Edom was famous for will not see it coming: “will I not destroy the wise men of Edom and the men of understanding in the mountains of Esau?” And the warriors follow the wise men. “Then your mighty men, O Teman, will be terrified, so that everyone in the mountains of Esau will be cut down in the slaughter.” So far the vision has named pride as the sin and total ruin as the end. It has not yet named the deed that earned it. That comes next, and it is not the pride.

title: You Should Not Have Gazed
subtitle: Obadiah 1
description: The charges are read: on Jerusalem's worst day, brother Edom gloated, looted, and hunted the fugitives.
paragraphs: Halfway through the vision, the reason for everything arrives in one sentence, and it is a family word. “Because of the violence against your brother Jacob, you will be covered with shame and cut off forever.” Not because of the pride, though the pride was real. Not because of the cliffs. Edom falls for what it did to its brother on the worst day of his life, and the shame and the cutting off are measured to that. The vision now stops announcing the fall and starts itemizing the day, act by act, the way a charge is read out.

The first charge is a posture. “On the day you stood aloof while strangers carried off his wealth and foreigners entered his gate and cast lots for Jerusalem, you were just like one of them.” Edom struck no blow in that sentence. It stood aloof, at a distance, and watched while foreigners looted its brother's city and gambled for Jerusalem like a prize. The verdict refuses to grade the distance. Standing apart while it happened made Edom one of the men doing it. Neutrality, on a brother's day of disaster, is entered into the record as participation.

Then the charges sharpen, and they come as things Edom should not have done, eight of them in a row. The first three are matters of the face and the mouth. “But you should not gloat in that day, your brother's day of misfortune, nor rejoice over the people of Judah in the day of their destruction, nor boast proudly in the day of their distress.” Gloating, rejoicing, boasting: Edom's first offenses were expressions. Before it moved a hand, it enjoyed what it saw, and said so, on the record, in the hearing of heaven. The day is named three times in one verse, your brother's day, the day of their destruction, the day of their distress, as if the calendar itself were evidence.

The next three move from the face to the feet and hands. “You should not enter the gate of My people in the day of their disaster, nor gloat over their affliction in the day of their disaster, nor loot their wealth in the day of their disaster.” The watcher has crossed the threshold. He is inside the gate now, looking at the affliction up close, and then his hands are in the wealth, taking what the strangers missed. Note whose people they are in God's sentence: My people. Edom entered the gate of God's own people on the day of their disaster and treated the disaster as an opportunity with a door left open.

The last two are the coldest. “Nor should you stand at the crossroads to cut off their fugitives, nor deliver up their survivors in the day of their distress.” Judah's people who escaped the city ran, and at the crossroads where the roads out of the ruin divided, their uncle's nation was waiting. Fugitives were cut off there. Survivors who got further were caught and handed over. The charges are complete: eyes that gloated, a mouth that boasted, feet that entered, hands that looted, and finally hands that hunted. What remains in the vision is the reckoning, and God has already chosen its measure: exactly what was done, returned.

title: The Kingdom Will Belong to the LORD
subtitle: Obadiah 1
description: The measure returns on every nation, Zion is restored, and the book ends: the kingdom belongs to the LORD.
paragraphs: The reckoning opens by widening past Edom. “For the Day of the LORD is near for all the nations.” What happened in the cliffs is about to become the pattern for everyone, and its rule is stated as a mirror: “As you have done, it will be done to you; your recompense will return upon your own head.” No new charges need inventing and no new penalties need designing. The deed itself is the sentence, turned around. Edom gloated over a brother drinking the cup of disaster; the vision now picks up the cup.

“For as you drank on My holy mountain, so all the nations will drink continually.” Edom had drunk in celebration on the mountain where God dwelt, in the city it looted. Now the drinking is handed to the nations as judgment, and it does not come in sips. “They will drink and gulp it down; they will be as if they had never existed.” The cup that was a party becomes an erasure. That is the fate of the nations in Edom's pattern. Then the vision turns, and the brother's mountain, the one Edom entered to loot, is described as it will be.

“But on Mount Zion there will be deliverance, and it will be holy, and the house of Jacob will reclaim their possession.” Everything Edom's day took apart is named restored in one verse: deliverance on the mountain, holiness on the mountain, and the dispossessed house holding its own again. And the brother nations meet as elements. “the house of Jacob will be a blazing fire, and the house of Joseph a burning flame; but the house of Esau will be stubble.” Fire does not negotiate with stubble. “Therefore no survivor will remain from the house of Esau.” The sentence lands, and over it stands the vision's guarantee: “For the LORD has spoken.”

Then the book spends its last verses on a map, and the map is drawn in every direction at once. “Those from the Negev will possess the mountains of Esau”, the very heights no one could take, held now by the people of the southern desert. The foothills' people will possess the land of the Philistines. “They will occupy the fields of Ephraim and Samaria, and Benjamin will possess Gilead.” The exiles get the widest lines of all: Israel's exiles “will possess the land of the Canaanites as far as Zarephath”, far up the coast, and “the exiles from Jerusalem who are in Sepharad will possess the cities of the Negev.” A people scattered to the edges comes home holding more than it lost, ring by ring, until the map is full.

The shortest book in the Bible ends on its largest sentence. “The deliverers will ascend Mount Zion to rule over the mountains of Esau. And the kingdom will belong to the LORD.” Rule over Esau's mountains is assigned, but it is not the last word; the last word is ownership, and the owner is God. Edom said in its heart that no one could bring it down. The vision's final answer is not only that someone could. It is that the kingdom was never Edom's, or Jacob's, to hold. It belongs to the LORD, and from that belonging everything else in the book, the fall and the restoration alike, takes its order.
